newsitem.title: SYRIA: Finland seeks better economic ties with Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Finland seeks better economic ties with Mideast.

text.p: Finland believes there are big investment opportunities in the Middle East and wants to boost its economic ties in the region, Ole Norrback, Finnish Minister for European Affairs and Foreign Trade, said on Tuesday.
Norrback, on a tour of Syria, Jordan and Lebanon at the head of a 20-member business team, said they came to increase the current limited trade with these states.
The minister, who first visited Jordan, told Reuters he expected the trip to pave the way for agreements on projects in energy production, telecommunications and food production sectors.
Norrback had talks with Syrian Economy and Foreign Trade Minister Mohammad Imadi and the Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Salim Yassin.
"During my talks in Syria I stressed the importance of moving towards the free market economy and free trade which will facilitate economic cooperation with other countries," the minister said.

"I can understand that countries like Syria want transition periods before their markets are opened. It is very easy to understand that but on the other hand free competition is always more in the consumer's interest," he said.
Syria, which for years had a socialist, state-controlled economy, five years ago started economic reform including a law to encourage private local and foreign investment.
Investors say they also want the value of the Syrian pound freed to reflect market valuation so investors would be encouraged to bring more hard currency to the country.

The Finnish minister said economic reform measures in Syria would pave the way for greator economic cooperation not only with Finland but also with the European Union, which is preparing for a new economic partnership with the Middle East countries.
Asked about his planned talks in Lebanon, the minister said Finland was keen to participate in the huge reconstruction plan to build up the country after 15 years of civil war ended in 1990.

"The Lebanon economy is increasing very rapidly and the investment (opportunity) is huge. If this process continues for some time Beirut will be again a business centre in this region," Norrback said.
